summary: The ustaz continues the story of the Prophet's ﷺ birth with his nursing: first by his mother Aminah and by Thuaibah, then by Halimah As-Sa'diyah from the village of Banu Sa'd. Halimah at first did not want to take the orphaned baby, but once he was in her arms, provision and blessing came to her in abundance. The ustaz explains why children were sent out of the city, to protect their health and shape their character and language among nature. He then compares this with our time through the book The Anxious Generation, and closes with suggestions for protecting our children's childhood.
keyPoints: Salawat is the only act of worship that Allah himself and the angels perform, and we are then commanded to do it.
Sending a baby to a wet nurse outside the city was common in many civilisations, and the stronger reason was to protect the child from early death.
Halimah at first did not want to take the Prophet ﷺ because he was an orphan, but blessing came as soon as he was in her arms.
Growing up among nature in Banu Sa'd protected the Prophet's ﷺ health, language and refinement of soul.
According to Jonathan Haidt, a childhood of play in nature has turned into a phone-based childhood, and this is linked to a rise in anxiety and depression.
Haidt's four recommendations: no smartphone before high school, no social media before 16, phone-free schools, and more unsupervised play.

chapters.title: The name Muhammad is praised without pause
chapters.summary: The ustaz recalls the previous episode on the Prophet's ﷺ birth and naming, and how his name is constantly mentioned and praised on earth.

chapters.title: Salawat, a special act of worship
chapters.summary: Allah and the angels send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and each of our salawat is delivered to him personally by an angel.

chapters.title: First nursing and the practice of wet nurses
chapters.summary: The Prophet ﷺ was first nursed by Aminah. Hiring wet nurses already existed among the Arabs, Greeks and Romans, especially in noble families.

chapters.title: Thuaibah and Hamzah RA
chapters.summary: While Abdul Muttalib looked for a wet nurse, Abu Lahab's slave Thuaibah nursed the Prophet ﷺ. Hamzah RA was also nursed by her.

chapters.title: Halimah and the village of Banu Sa'd
chapters.summary: Halimah's story is recorded in Sirah Ibn Hisham. She came from the village of Banu Sa'd, far from the city life of Mecca.

chapters.title: Why children were sent out of the city
chapters.summary: The stronger reason was to protect babies from early death by disease. The ustaz links it to how common infant death was before vaccines and modern medicine.

chapters.title: Halimah comes to Mecca in a drought
chapters.summary: Halimah set out with other women while the village suffered a drought, on a weak camel, and arrived last.

chapters.title: The orphan nobody wanted to take
chapters.summary: All the other babies had been taken. The wet nurses turned the Prophet ﷺ down because his father had died and they feared the payment would be held up.

chapters.title: A restless night and Halimah's decision
chapters.summary: Halimah could not sleep because her baby kept crying and she did not have enough milk. In the end she decided to take the Prophet ﷺ, and her husband reassured her.

chapters.title: Blessing arrives with the Prophet ﷺ
chapters.summary: As soon as Halimah received him, her milk came in and the camel that had run dry began to fill, and the journey home was full of wonders.

chapters.title: Growing up among nature in Banu Sa'd
chapters.summary: Life in the midst of nature protected health and shaped character and a refined soul. The ustaz cites Shaykh Muhammad Al-Ghazali in Fiqh as-Sirah.

chapters.title: The Anxious Generation and Jonathan Haidt
chapters.summary: The ustaz introduces Haidt's thesis that a childhood of play has turned into a phone-based childhood, with a surge of anxiety and depression after 2010.

chapters.title: The Prophet's ﷺ language and the first two recommendations
chapters.summary: The Prophet ﷺ had his language preserved in Banu Sa'd. The ustaz lists the recommendations of no smartphone before high school and no social media before 16.

chapters.title: Phone-free schools and room to play
chapters.summary: The third and fourth recommendations are phone-free schools and more unsupervised play. Excessive fear stops children from exploring with courage.

chapters.title: The effect in schools and universities
chapters.summary: The experience of teachers, wardens and lecturers shows high levels of anxiety and depression among students. The ustaz stresses our shared responsibility to act.

chapters.title: The first three years and closing
chapters.summary: The ustaz cites Gabor Maté's advice on the importance of the first three years, and promises the next episode on the Prophet's ﷺ return to his mother.

books.context: Records Halimah's story at length, and is an abridgement of Sirah Ibn Ishaq.
books.note: Author not named in the lecture: Ibn Hisham

books.context: Says that the Prophet ﷺ and Hamzah shared two wet nurses, Thuaibah and Halimah.
Has a chapter interpreting the names around the Prophet ﷺ, all of which carry good meanings.
The author expresses sadness for children today who grow up far from nature.
books.note: Title given in the lecture as Fekusirah

books.context: Investigates why anxiety, depression and self-harm have risen among children since 2010. The ustaz recommends the site theanxiousgeneration.com for free material.

people.context: Nursed him for a day or two after birth. The ustaz mentions one view that her health did not allow continued nursing.

people.role: Abu Lahab's slave and the Prophet's ﷺ first wet nurse
people.context: Nursed the Prophet ﷺ while nursing her own son Masruh, and also nursed Hamzah RA.
Looked for a wet nurse for him, and according to one report met Halimah and suggested she nurse him.

people.role: Companion and uncle of the Prophet ﷺ
people.context: Also nursed by Thuaibah, and according to one report was also sent to the village of Banu Sa'd.

people.role: Scholar and author of Zad al-Ma'ad
people.context: Says that the Prophet ﷺ and Hamzah shared two wet nurses.

people.role: Wet nurse of the Prophet ﷺ
people.context: A woman of Banu Sa'd who ended up taking the Prophet ﷺ, and her family received blessing. The ustaz mentions the possibility that she accepted Islam late in life.
The name of Halimah's son according to some sirah reports; he also nursed well beside the Prophet ﷺ.
Reassured Halimah by saying that Allah might give provision by another route when she took the Prophet ﷺ.
In his book he interprets the meanings of the names around the Prophet ﷺ: Aminah (security), Shaybat al-Hamd (the praised), Barakah (blessing) and Halimah (hilm, patient and gentle).

people.role: Scholar, teacher of Shaykh Yusuf Al-Qaradawi
people.context: The ustaz stresses he is not Imam Al-Ghazali. He wrote Fiqh as-Sirah and expressed sadness about children who are far from nature.

people.role: Social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation
people.context: Studies how childhood has changed and links the surge of mental health problems after 2010 to a phone-based childhood.
Asked the Prophet ﷺ about the refinement of his language, and he said he was nursed in Banu Sa'd.

people.role: Active in the rehabilitation of teenage girls
people.context: The ustaz often engages with her and hears the stories of the teens she helps, and concludes that no one is fully safe from these challenges.
The ustaz cites his advice that the effort to protect a child's first three years has an effect on the years that follow.

lessons.title: Salawat is a special act of worship
lessons.body: Allah and the angels send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and we are then commanded to do the same, and each of our salawat is delivered to him.

lessons.title: Understand the sirah in the context of its time
lessons.body: The sirah cannot be viewed through today's lens, for example the desire for sons and the practice of wet nurses in that era.

lessons.title: Be thankful for today's health
lessons.body: In the past, giving birth and raising a child risked life itself. Today medical progress saves most children, and that deserves gratitude.

lessons.title: Provision comes from unexpected routes
lessons.body: Halimah's husband reassured her that Allah might give provision from another route, and that is what happened.

lessons.title: Empathy and calm in the family
lessons.body: Halimah's husband showed empathy by calming his wife, and Halimah's hilm made her heart at ease.

lessons.title: Nature shapes the soul and character
lessons.body: Playing among nature, clouds, mountains and rivers shapes character and a refinement of soul that connects the heart to Allah's creation.

lessons.title: Children are a trust
lessons.body: Children are a trust we will be asked about, so parents need to find ways to give them a better life.

lessons.title: Technology has its time and stage
lessons.body: Technology has many benefits, but it should not be forced on children early. Give it when the child is ready, with self-confidence and emotional foundations.

lessons.title: Do not let fear stop children from exploring
lessons.body: One or two incidents should not be over-generalised until children are kept at home with screens, when screens have their own dangers.

lessons.title: A shared duty to protect childhood
lessons.body: Parents, schools and society all have a part in making sure children grow up with a healthy childhood.

lessons.title: The first three years are decisive
lessons.body: Strive to protect a child's childhood from the start, because early neglect will need remedying for the rest of their lives.

glossary.meaning: Prayers and praise for the Prophet ﷺ. Allah and the angels send blessings on him, and we are commanded to do so.
A woman paid to nurse and care for another's child, common among noble families.
Halimah's home village, far from the city life of Mecca and known for its pure Arabic.
A sacrifice marking a child's birth, recommended on the seventh day along with giving the name.
Apparent causes, while Allah decides the outcome. The ustaz says Halimah would have received the Prophet ﷺ whatever the causes.
Blessing, meaning goodness that increases and is felt in provision and life.
Great patience, being caring and gentle in feeling, as in the meaning of the name Halimah.

dalil.context: Allah and the angels send blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, and believers are commanded to send blessings on him. (reference identified; verse number not mentioned)
dalil.translation: God and His angels bless the Prophet- so, you who believe, bless him too and give him greetings of peace.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it as an interesting point about salawat, and our salawat reaches him wherever we are.
dalil.translation: Whenever someone sends blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, an angel is sent specifically to deliver that salawat to him.

dalil.context: The ustaz links this hadith to the conditions of that era, when many babies did not live past early childhood.
dalil.translation: Sacrifice the aqiqah and name the child on the seventh day or before.

dalil.context: The ustaz mentions it as a sign that the Banu Sa'd environment preserved the purity of the Prophet's ﷺ Arabic.
dalil.translation: The Prophet ﷺ said that he was nursed in the village of Banu Sa'd, when answering Abu Bakr's question about the refinement of his language.
